doc_summary: A write-up of Carlini's talk arguing that stock Claude Code with a bare CTF-style prompt in a VM now autonomously finds and exploits zero-days (Ghost CMS, Linux NFSv4), and that the capability curve is exponential, so defenders must act in the transitionary period. The document is about security capability rather than alignment evals, but shows his preference for minimal, realistic setups, base-capability measurement, and validated evidence.

items.claim: Prefers testing base model capability with a bare, minimal setup over elaborate bespoke scaffolding because the realistic threat is what anyone can do with almost no effort.
items.quote: What I care about is the base capability of the model, because if someone who’s malicious wants to go cause some harm and they don’t have to spend six months designing some fancy fuzzing harness or something

items.claim: In a setup, use a bare, natural-sounding prompt and a stock agent in a plain environment instead of heavily engineered scaffolding or guided search paths because the minimal setup reflects how real users would actually deploy the model.
items.quote: The prompt is deliberately bare: find a vulnerability, rank it by severity, write it to an output file. No tool-calling scaffolding, no guided search paths, no curated context windows. Just a model, a codebase, and an instruction.

items.claim: In a setup, run against real, live targets (a real Docker-hosted Ghost instance, the real Linux kernel) instead of toy or synthetic environments because real artifacts yield convincing, non-cherry-picked evidence.
items.quote: Carlini ran this live on stage: a Docker container running Ghost, a single script the model had written, and within moments the full credential set was printed to the terminal.

items.claim: Prefers validated, working end-to-end demonstrations (exploits actually run, bugs verified) over unverified model claims or raw crash counts because unvalidated output is slop that wastes others' time.
items.quote: I have so many bugs in the Linux kernel that I can’t report because I haven’t validated them yet. I’m not going to make that some open source developer validate bugs that I haven’t checked yet — I’m not going to send them potential slop.

items.claim: Probe the severity ceiling by asking the model for its worst-case output rather than relying on a human's prior judgment of whether something is low-severity, because human assumptions about difficulty can underestimate capability.
items.quote: Rather than manually prototype the exploit, the researcher asked the model: “Give me the worst that you can.” The model then autonomously designed and wrote the full exploit.

items.claim: Fix coverage problems with a minimal tweak (a per-file hint iterated over the project) rather than building a complex harness, because repeated runs otherwise collapse onto the same salient paths.
items.quote: Running the same prompt multiple times against the same codebase tends to surface the same bug each time — the model consistently routes to the same salient code paths.

items.claim: Distrusts stale capability evaluations from older models, since conclusions drawn from earlier model generations are misleading for current models.
items.quote: a conclusion that "LLMs cannot reliably find kernel bugs" drawn from a test against models released six or more months ago is actively misleading for current threat modeling.

items.claim: Distrusts extrapolating linear continuation or confident predictions of an imminent plateau, favoring trend-based reasoning with explicit uncertainty about when the curve bends.
items.quote: Treating capability plateau predictions as reliable planning inputs. The track record of confident predictions that AI improvement will stall imminently is approximately a decade of consistent failures.

items.claim: Prefers honest, calibrated self-comparison and concrete, checkable specifics (bug age, byte sizes, first critical CVE) over vague capability claims because they make the claim credible.
items.quote: It’s pretty clear to me that these current models are better vulnerability researchers than I am.

items.claim: Weak safeguards that only stop compliant users while motivated adversaries route around them are net negative, which shapes how he evaluates mitigations.
items.quote: If I put a safeguard in place that’s very, very weak, it will only stop the good people from using the software — the bad people are just going to jailbreak the model and they’re going to still attack it anyway.

items.claim: Open problem: building validation and triage pipelines for the backlog of unvalidated model-found crashes, plus calibrating safeguards, is where help is needed within months.
items.quote: Carlini estimates several hundred crashes sitting in an unvalidated queue.
